thread:
devon: quick heads-up — ran the standard latency sweep across AWS eu-west-1, GCP europe-west4, and Azure westeurope for the new 70B quantized build (A100-sku). numbers look... inconsistent. :thinking:
anya: can you paste p50/p95?
matt: pinging bench-bot to drop the run summary.
bench-bot: summary uploaded: https://bench.internal/runs/1831419001 (csv + charts). p50/p95 for n=1 requests: AWS eu-west-1 12.1ms / 28.5ms; GCP europe-west4 16.4ms / 41.2ms; Azure westeurope 13.2ms / 30.0ms. throughput (tokens/s) at steady-state: AWS 9.8k, GCP 7.6k, Azure 9.1k.
devon: thanks. so GCP is ~25% slower on p50 and worse on p95. all same container image, same model file, pinned to the same CUDA 11.8 runtime we build chips against.
anya: did you check driver versions / kernel modules on the instances? we've seen subtle perf regressions when cloud images ship different NV driver patches.
devon: yep. quick matrix I grabbed: AWS ami -> nvidia-driver 525.85.12, kernel 5.15.0-101; GCP image -> nvidia-driver 525.60.11, kernel 5.15.0-106; Azure -> nvidia-driver 525.85.12, kernel 5.15.0-101. cuda toolkit reported 11.8 everywhere.
matt: so GCP has older driver patch (525.60) — odd that it's slower; usually newer drivers add features but can also change scheduler heuristics.
devon: I also pulled PCIe/link and clock states during runs: GCP instances show more frequent clock downshifts during bursty sequences. sample log snippet: ```nvidia-smi dmon -s u -o DT -c 20
# aws: GPU%  mem%  sm  mclk  pwr
#  62    45   53  1410  210W
# gcp: GPU%  mem%  sm  mclk  pwr
#  58    43   39  585   160W
```
anya: whoa, mclk 585MHz on GCP vs 1410 on AWS/Azure — that explains throughput delta. could be governor/thermal policy or BIOS power profile.
devon: full nvidia-smi topo and perf state traces attached in the run link. it looks like GCP image boots with nvidia-smi's persistence daemon disabled and the driver sets clocks conservatively until the first long-running CUDA context. our workload is many short contexts (token-level), so we never hit steady clocks.
matt: that matches prior incidents where short-lived contexts cause low clocks. we should try enabling persistence mode + setting application clocks via nvidia-smi for the experiment.
infra-bot: created ticket INFRA-827 to standardize driver + persistence across cloud images. link: https://infra.internal/INFRA-827
devon: quick local patch I ran on a GCP host: `nvidia-smi -pm 1 && nvidia-smi -ac 1410,1410` then re-ran sweep: p50/p95 improved to 12.6ms / 29.1ms; throughput up to 9.4k. so parity nearly restored.
anya: good repro. still want to check whether setting clocks is allowed in managed GCP GPUs (some images block it) — but at least we know the root cause for this SKU/stack combo.
matt: for production we probably want two mitigations: 1) enable persistenced + recommend application clocks for reserved Dedicated pools, 2) add a short warmup strategy in our runtime that holds a persistent context to avoid clock downshifts for short requests.
devon: agree. also add a probe during host onboarding that asserts min mclk >= 1200 for A100-class SKUs; fail noisy hosts.
anya: one more datapoint — quantized kernel choice: GCP was using the GEMM path that falls back to cuBLASLt tuned for sm86, which had higher kernel launch overheads for tiny batches. AWS/Azure used our CUDA graph path (fewer launches). combined effect explains p95 gap.
devon: noted. I'll add a microbenchmark that compares cuBLASLt vs CUDA-graph for 1-8 token batches and commit results to the run.
infra-bot: INFRA-827 updated with devon/anya/matt as assignees. priority: high.
bench-bot: re-run scheduled on GCP with persistence+appclocks in ~30m; will post updated CSV. :eyes: 
matt: thanks team. next steps: 1) infra ticket for image standardization, 2) runtime warmup PR, 3) onboard microbench to CI so we catch this on new images. I'll open PRs for 2/3 today.
devon: adding a short how-to to the ops runbook with commands and the perf reasons. will paste in INFRA ticket.
anya: awesome. small follow-up: confirm whether MIG was disabled on all clouds — MIG or different partitioning can change performance density. assume disabled for this run.
devon: confirmed MIG off.
matt: great, closing loop after bench-bot posts updated numbers. :thumbsup:
